title: The Voltage Divider That Collapsed Under Load
featured_title: THE VOLTAGE DIVIDER THAT COLLAPSED UNDER LOAD
subject: electrical-computer
audience: FE Electrical and Computer candidates and engineering students

presentation.challenge: The divider measured exactly 6 V with no load. Connect one load, and the output falls to 4 V.

case_dna.target_misconception: A voltage-divider output stays fixed after a finite load is connected because the two divider resistors themselves have not changed.
case_dna.why_plausible: Students often memorize the unloaded divider formula and treat the output node as if it were an ideal voltage source. A finite load becomes part of the lower leg and changes the network being solved.
case_dna.contradicting_evidence: A 10 kΩ load placed across the 10 kΩ lower divider resistor makes the effective lower leg 5 kΩ, so the output becomes 12 × 5/(10+5) = 4 V rather than 6 V.
case_dna.corrected_model: Before applying the voltage-divider equation, include the connected load in the circuit model. Reduce the loaded lower leg to its equivalent resistance, then calculate the divider output.

problem_statement: A 12 V source feeds a divider made from a 10 kΩ top resistor and a 10 kΩ lower resistor. The midpoint measures 6 V with no load. A 10 kΩ load is then connected from the midpoint to ground, and the output falls to 4 V. Diagnose why the unloaded calculation no longer applies and choose a correction that restores 6 V for this known load.
fixed_constraints: Load remains 10 kΩ from output to ground

gates.label: Incident
gates.heading: The divider was correct until the load was connected.
facts: Connected load: 10 kΩ from midpoint to ground
gates.prompt: The source and divider resistors did not change. What did the load change in the circuit model?

gates.label: Theory
gates.heading: Choose the best explanation before reducing the network

options.label: The load is in parallel with the lower resistor and changes the divider ratio
options.reason: This is the loaded-network model. The lower 10 kΩ resistor in parallel with the 10 kΩ load becomes 5 kΩ, so the divider ratio changes.

options.label: The 12 V source must have dropped to 8 V when the load was connected
options.reason: The case states the source remains 12 V. The output change is explained by the added load changing the lower-leg equivalent resistance.

options.label: The output should remain 6 V because the two divider resistors are still 10 kΩ each
options.reason: This ignores the load. Once connected, the load is electrically in parallel with the lower resistor, so the actual lower leg is no longer 10 kΩ.

options.label: The 4 V reading must be a meter error because the unloaded divider formula gives 6 V
options.reason: The 4 V reading matches the loaded-circuit calculation exactly. The error is applying an unloaded model to a loaded network.

gates.label: Predict
gates.heading: Predict the loaded output before calculating it
gates.prompt: With a 10 kΩ load connected across the 10 kΩ lower resistor, what output voltage (V) do you expect?

gates.label: Experiment
gates.heading: Connect the 10 kΩ load
gates.result: The midpoint settles at 4 V with the 10 kΩ load connected, even though it was 6 V unloaded.

gates.label: Gap
gates.heading: Prove the loaded output
gates.prompt: First reduce the lower leg: 10 kΩ || 10 kΩ = 5 kΩ. Then calculate Vout = 12 × 5/(10+5). Enter the loaded output voltage.
gates.hint: The load is in parallel with the lower divider resistor. Reduce that pair before using the divider equation.

gates.label: Evidence
gates.heading: The reduced circuit shows what changed

cards.text: Lower leg under load: 10 kΩ || 10 kΩ = 5 kΩ.
The 12 V source and the original two divider resistor values remain unchanged.

gates.label: Redline
gates.heading: Correct the design note
report: C1. A 12 V source with two equal 10 kΩ divider resistors produces 6 V when unloaded.
C2. A 10 kΩ load is connected from the midpoint to ground.
C3. Because the two divider resistors are still equal, the output remains 6 V after the load is connected.

claims.label: C1
claims.reason: C1 is correct for the unloaded divider: equal resistors split 12 V to 6 V.

claims.label: C2
claims.reason: C2 is a stated connection fact and is part of the loaded-circuit model.

claims.label: C3
claims.reason: C3 ignores the load's electrical effect. The load parallels the lower resistor, changing the effective lower leg from 10 kΩ to 5 kΩ and the output from 6 V to 4 V.

evidence_choices.label: The loaded lower leg is 10 kΩ || 10 kΩ = 5 kΩ, giving 4 V output
evidence_choices.reason: This directly shows why the 6 V unloaded result no longer applies: the lower-leg resistance and divider ratio changed under load.

evidence_choices.label: The source remains 12 V
evidence_choices.reason: This rules out source sag as the explanation, but it does not by itself show why the divider output becomes 4 V.

evidence_choices.label: The original top resistor is still 10 kΩ
evidence_choices.reason: The top resistor staying unchanged is true, but the load changes the lower leg, which is the missing part of the model.

correction.template: With the 10 kΩ load connected, the effective lower resistance is {lower_eq} kΩ and the loaded output is {loaded_v} V — not 6 V.

gates.label: Design Fix
gates.heading: Restore 6 V for the known 10 kΩ load
gates.constraint: Keep the 12 V source, the 10 kΩ load, and a passive two-resistor divider.

options.label: Use a 5 kΩ top resistor and a 10 kΩ lower resistor
options.reason: With the 10 kΩ load, the lower leg is 10 kΩ || 10 kΩ = 5 kΩ. A 5 kΩ top resistor and 5 kΩ effective lower leg split 12 V equally, producing 6 V under the stated load.

options.label: Keep 10 kΩ top and 10 kΩ lower resistors
options.reason: Under the 10 kΩ load, the effective lower leg remains 5 kΩ, so the loaded output remains 4 V.

options.label: Increase the top resistor to 20 kΩ and keep the lower resistor at 10 kΩ
options.reason: The loaded lower leg is still 5 kΩ, so Vout becomes 12 × 5/(20+5) = 2.4 V, farther from the 6 V requirement.

options.label: Disconnect the 10 kΩ load whenever 6 V is required
options.reason: That restores the unloaded 6 V only by violating the requirement that the 10 kΩ load remain connected.

gates.label: Transfer
gates.heading: Apply the loading rule to a new divider
gates.prompt: A divider has a finite load connected from its output node to ground. Compared with the unloaded case, what usually happens when that load is comparable to the lower divider resistance?

options.label: The output drops because the effective lower resistance decreases
options.reason: A finite load in parallel with the lower resistor reduces the effective lower-leg resistance and therefore reduces the divider ratio.

options.label: The output stays exactly the same because the divider resistors did not change
options.reason: The load becomes part of the network. The original divider resistors may be unchanged physically, but the effective lower-leg resistance changes.

options.label: The output always rises because another resistor was added
options.reason: A load from output to ground parallels the lower resistor, reducing that resistance and normally lowering the output voltage.

options.label: The output must become zero for any finite load
options.reason: A finite load changes the divider ratio, but it does not short the output unless the load resistance approaches zero.

gates.explanation: A finite load connected across the lower divider resistor reduces the effective lower resistance and changes the divider ratio.

gates.label: Sign Off
gates.heading: Sign off the loaded-divider analysis
gates.confirmation: I confirm that the connected load must be included in the circuit model before applying the voltage-divider equation.

items.label: What changed
items.value: The 10 kΩ load paralleled the 10 kΩ lower resistor, reducing the effective lower leg to 5 kΩ.

items.label: What was missed
items.value: The unloaded divider formula was applied after the load changed the network.

items.label: Corrected model
items.value: Reduce the actual loaded network first, then calculate Vout from the resulting divider ratio.

seo.seo_title: Voltage Divider Loading Effect: Why 6 V Drops to 4 V | FE E-019
seo.meta_description: Solve FE Case E-019: a 12 V, 10 kΩ–10 kΩ divider gives 6 V unloaded but 4 V with a 10 kΩ load. Diagnose the loading effect and fix it.
seo.focus_keyphrase: voltage divider loading effect FE exam
seo.excerpt: A divider can be mathematically correct when unloaded and still miss its target once a finite load is connected. Diagnose why 6 V falls to 4 V.
seo.direct_answer: A finite load changes a voltage divider because it becomes part of the lower leg. Here, a 10 kΩ load in parallel with the 10 kΩ lower resistor gives 5 kΩ, so Vout = 12 × 5/(10+5) = 4 V instead of 6 V.

faqs.q: Why does a voltage divider output drop under load?
faqs.a: A load connected from the output to ground is in parallel with the lower divider resistor. That reduces the effective lower resistance and changes the divider ratio.

faqs.q: What is 10 kΩ in parallel with 10 kΩ?
How do you calculate a loaded voltage divider?
faqs.a: First combine the load with the resistor it parallels, then use that equivalent resistance in the voltage-divider equation.

practice.primary_question: Why does a voltage divider output change when a finite load is connected?
practice.typical_exam_trap: Using the unloaded divider formula after a finite load has changed the lower-leg resistance.
